What finite geometry is allowed to say about particles

29 July 2026 · programme note

A finite geometry should do more than provide an attractive container for a list of particles. It should explain which algebra, representations, one-forms, and scalar sectors are permitted, and where the construction fails.

Particle models are naturally described by finite internal data: algebras acting on a Hilbert space, a grading and real structure, and a finite Dirac operator that links different sectors. The temptation is to choose these ingredients until the desired field content appears. The more interesting question runs in the opposite direction. Begin with a rigid algebraic input and ask what the axioms and calculi force.

Two developing routes

One current route starts from Clifford and octonionic structure. A Cℓ6 construction organizes a one-generation finite Hilbert space through Peirce and ladder decompositions, with charge generators and scalar data emerging from the representation. The immediate task is not to advertise a completed phenomenological model. It is to determine exactly which finite-triple conditions are satisfied, which scalar sectors are generated, and which completions or obstructions remain.

A second route, developed in the Quantum Riemannian Geometry programme, begins with quaternionic calculi and linked finite spaces. Cocycle-twisted quaternionic geometry supplies differential, metric, Hodge, and Dirac data. Linking a complex sector to a quaternionic one then gives a controlled setting in which scalar- quaternionic links, gauge quotients, and electroweak-style channels can be tested rather than assumed.

Claims must follow the calculation

The useful outputs are therefore structural: classification of finite one-forms, inner fluctuations, allowed link fields, scalar potentials, real-structure constraints, unimodularity conditions, and no-go results. Some outcomes may resemble familiar particle sectors; others may show that a tempting construction is too rigid or not rigid enough.

This branch of the research programme is intentionally future-facing. Its public claims should remain behind its calculations. The ambition is to build a finite-geometric route in which particle-sector organization is earned step by step, while keeping a visible distinction between what the geometry has forced and what a model builder has chosen.

The near-public Cℓ6 finite-triple manuscript and the linked C ⊕ H programme are listed on the research page as programme anchors, not as published results.
